title: Overview
text:
Overview VxLang — Windows Binary Protection, Code Obfuscation & Virtualization VxLang is a binary protection solution designed to make reverse engineering and tampering with Windows executables more difficult. It combines technologies such as executable packing, code obfuscation, code virtualization, control-flow flattening, and Runtime Code Encryption to protect important code and data. VxLang supports both protecting existing compiled binaries and selecting code regions for protection directly through its SDK . Users can choose the protection methods that best suit their applications and performance requirements. Note: VxLang is designed to increase the difficulty of analysis and tampering. It does not guarantee complete prevention of every form of reverse engineering or memory dumping. Protection effectiveness and compatibility depend on the target application, configuration, and runtime environment. 1. Key Features Packer & Protector Protects the distribution format and loading process of an executable. Executable packing and optional compression Entry point protection Import table mutation Anti-tamper checks and memory protection options Integration of protected code and runtime features through VxLang-Core Packing helps conceal the original executable structure and complicate analysis. However, unpacking an executable does not necessarily mean recovering its original code . Obfuscation, virtualization, and Runtime Code Encryption provide additional, independent layers of protection. Code Obfuscation Transforms instruction representations and code structures while preserving the original behavior. Instruction and code-pattern transformations Arithmetic and logic obfuscation, including MBA techniques Protection of individual functions or selected code regions Protection core selection ( phobos / deimos , depending on version and compatibility) Obfuscation is intended to increase the difficulty of static analysis and automated code understanding. Code Virtualization Converts selected native code into a form executed by the VxLang virtual machine (VM). Execution through a virtual instruction set and VM handlers Function-level or region-based virtualization Dual-Mode protection combining obfuscation and virtualization Advanced configurations such as multiple VMs and TMA Virtualization (in supported versions) Virtualization is suitable for protecting critical logic, but it may affect execution speed and binary size. For performance-sensitive applications, it is generally better to apply virtualization selectively to critical code rather than to the entire program. Code Flattening Transforms a program's control flow to make branches and execution paths more difficult to trace. Transformation of branch structures and control-flow graphs (CFGs) Selective application to functions and code regions Supported methods such as REpsych Code Flattening Runtime Code Encryption Decrypts selected code regions only when they are needed at runtime, then re-encrypts them after execution of the protected region is complete. Keeps protected code encrypted in the distributed binary Decrypts code when entering a protected region and re-encrypts it upon exit Reference-counted operation to handle overlapping access from multiple threads Makes collecting plaintext code through memory dumps more difficult VxLang-Core must be loaded for code protected with Runtime Code Encryption to execute. As a result, removing the packer shell alone does not mean that the original code in encrypted regions can be successfully restored or executed. However, decrypted code is present in memory while it is executing. Runtime Code Encryption therefore does not completely eliminate the possibility of dynamic analysis during that interval. 2. How VxLang Works VxLang takes a target binary and its protection configuration as input, then generates an output file with the selected protection features applied. TEXT Copy [Original EXE / DLL / PE]
            |
            v
 [Protection Configuration]
     |       |       |
     |       |       +-- SDK Markers / Function Selection
     |       +---------- JSON / CLI Options
     +------------------ Obscurion (GUI)
            |
            v
        [VxLang]
     |      |       |
     |      |       +-- Code Virtualization / Dual-Mode
     |      +---------- Obfuscation / Code Flattening
     +----------------- Packer / Protector / Runtime Code Encryption*
            |
            v
     [Protected Binary]
            |
            v
 [Execution with VxLang-Core*]

* Requirements depend on the selected features and configuration. Different protection layers may be applied to different parts of a protected executable. Protection Method Primary Purpose Example Target Packer / Protector Protect file structure and loading behavior Entire executable Obfuscation Transform instructions and code representation Functions and code regions Virtualization Convert code to a VM instruction set License checks, critical algorithms Code Flattening Complicate control flow Functions with important branching logic Runtime Code Encryption Reduce the time code is exposed in plaintext Sensitive code sections Multiple methods can be used together, but it is important to balance protection strength, performance, and compatibility . 3. VxLang-Core VxLang-Core is a core component that supports packing and runtime protection features in protected executables. Depending on the configuration, it is used to execute protected code and support certain SDK integrations and extended protection features. Supports the execution process of protected binaries Integrates with VxLang runtime protection features Works with relevant SDK events and protected regions Is required for runtime code decryption when using Runtime Code Encryption Some obfuscation and virtualization configurations can be evaluated without VxLang-Core by using disable-core . However, features that depend on VxLang-Core may not function correctly in this configuration . In particular, when Runtime Code Encryption is used, removing VxLang-Core prevents the expected decryption and execution of encrypted code regions. Refer to the configuration reference for your VxLang version for the exact behavior and supported combinations of disable-core . 4. Protection Methods The main VxLang protection technologies have different purposes and operating principles. Category Packer Obfuscator Virtualizer Runtime Code Encryption Main Role Protect files and loading Transform code representation Convert native execution to VM-based execution Decrypt code when needed at runtime Typical Scope Entire binary Selected regions Selected regions Selected regions Analysis Resistance Conceals original file structure Increases the difficulty of understanding static code Increases the difficulty of recovering native logic Reduces plaintext code exposure time Considerations Loading and compatibility Code size and performance Execution performance Concurrent execution and VxLang-Core dependency Recommended approach: Apply an appropriate level of packing protection to the executable, selectively use obfuscation or virtualization for critical algorithms, and consider Runtime Code Encryption for regions where plaintext exposure during execution should be minimized. 5. Supported Platforms VxLang primarily targets Microsoft Windows PE (Portable Executable) files . Target Description Windows EXE Protection for standard executable files Windows DLL Protection for dynamic-link libraries Windows SYS Features for kernel drivers; available protection methods may be restricted UEFI Features for UEFI PE binaries; environment-specific limitations may apply .NET EXE Protection through a separate extension module such as ExtsDN The primary target architectures are x86 and x64 . Windows ARM64 and Linux ELF are under consideration for development or expansion, so support should be verified against the version currently in use. Even when a file type is supported, not all protection features are necessarily available for it. Kernel, UEFI, and .NET environments have different requirements from standard Windows user-mode applications. 6. Ways to Use VxLang VxLang offers three main ways to configure and apply protection. Method Description Recommended For Obscurion (GUI) Visually configure the target binary, functions, and protection options First-time users VxLang CLI Run protection tasks with command-line options or JSON configuration files Automation and build pipelines VxLang SDK Select protected code regions directly in source code C/C++ application developers For example, the SDK can be used to mark a code region inside a function: CPP Copy void ProtectedFunction () { VL_VIRTUALIZATION_BEGIN ; // Protect this code region. ImportantOperation (); VL_VIRTUALIZATION_END ; } This example illustrates the SDK marker syntax. Actual compilation and protection require the appropriate SDK headers and libraries, as well as the VxLang build step. The final boundaries of a protected region may also be affected by compiler optimizations. 7. Limitations & Considerations Before applying protection, review the following considerations. Compatibility testing is necessary. Exception handling (C++ EH/SEH), compiler optimizations, threading, and runtime characteristics may require adjustments to the protected regions. Performance overhead is possible. Virtualization and intensive obfuscation should generally be applied selectively to critical regions. SDK boundaries may not exactly match source-code boundaries. Verify the final binary with compiler optimizations, inlining, and function merging in mind. Plaintext exposure during execution remains possible. Even with Runtime Code Encryption, analysis may target the moments when protected code is decrypted and running. Feature support depends on the version and environment. Check the selected plugins, architecture, target file format, and any dependencies on VxLang-Core. 8. Next Steps If you are new to VxLang, we recommend following these steps: Getting Started — Prepare the application components and license. Using Obscurion (GUI) — Apply protection settings to your first executable. Protection Features — Choose the most suitable method for each part of your application. SDK Integration — Define protected regions directly in critical functions. Advanced Configuration — Fine-tune performance, compatibility, and advanced protection options. Official resources VxLang Documentation VxLang GitHub

title: Purchase
text: Purchase VxLang offers Subscription Licenses and Named Licenses (Lifetime Licenses) to accommodate different user needs. 1. New User License The New User License is designed for users who are new to VxLang. Includes a one-year subscription. Provides access to the latest versions and updates throughout the subscription period. The license is valid for one year and can be freely renewed. This is not a Named License (Lifetime License). If you are subscribing to VxLang for the first time, you must purchase the New User License first. Purchase New User License 2. Personal Subscription The Personal Subscription is a subscription license for existing individual users. Users who have purchased the New User License can extend their VxLang subscription through the Personal Subscription. Extend the validity period of your existing license. Access the latest versions and updates throughout the subscription period. No need to purchase the New User License again. Important Notice The Personal Subscription is available only to users who have purchased the New User License. If you purchase a Personal Subscription without first purchasing the New User License, you will not be granted access to VxLang, and your subscription payment will be refunded. New users must purchase the New User License first. Personal Subscription 3. Named License The Named License is a lifetime license that allows you to use VxLang indefinitely without a recurring subscription. Named Licenses are available in two categories: Personal and Team. 3.1. Personal Named License A lifetime license for individual developers and personal users. One-time purchase. No license expiration date. Lifetime use without a recurring subscription. Price: $499 USD 3.2. Team Named License A lifetime license designed for companies, development teams, and environments where multiple developers use VxLang. One-time purchase. No license expiration date. Team-based licensing. Pricing and licensing terms for the Team Named License are available upon request. Price: Contact Us If you are interested in purchasing a Team Named License, please contact the developer directly. 4. License Comparison License Validity Period Price Intended Users New User License 1 year See purchase page New users Personal Subscription Subscription period See subscription page Existing individual users Personal Named License Lifetime $499 USD Individual users Team Named License Lifetime Contact Us Companies and development teams 5. Purchase Process Subscription License Purchase the New User License. Download VxLang and set up your license. Use VxLang for one year. Extend your subscription through the Personal Subscription. Named License Select either a Personal or Team Named License. Contact the developer regarding your license purchase. Receive your license. Use VxLang indefinitely. 6. Frequently Asked Questions Can new users purchase a Personal Subscription directly? No. New subscribers must purchase the New User License first. If you purchase a Personal Subscription without first purchasing the New User License, you will not be granted access to VxLang, and your payment will be refunded. Is the New User License a lifetime license? No. The New User License includes a one-year subscription, which can be extended through additional subscriptions. Do I need to purchase the New User License again after one year? No. After your initial purchase, you can extend your subscription through the Personal Subscription. Can I use VxLang without a recurring subscription? Yes. By purchasing a Named License, you can use VxLang indefinitely without a recurring subscription. Do I need a New User License to purchase a Named License? No. Named Licenses are offered separately from Subscription Licenses. How can I purchase a Team Named License? Please contact the developer directly to purchase a Team Named License. 7. Official Purchase Pages VxLang Official Shop VxLang Official Patreon

title: Getting Started
text:
Getting Started Getting Started with VxLang — From downloading VxLang to protecting your first Windows executable This guide is intended for first-time VxLang users. It explains how to prepare VxLang, select an EXE file, create a protected executable, and verify that it runs correctly. VxLang can protect already compiled Windows binaries, so you do not need to integrate an SDK or modify source code for your first test. Function-level obfuscation, virtualization, and Runtime Code Encryption are covered in subsequent guides. Contents Download & Purchase — Purchasing and downloading VxLang Installation & File Structure — Installation and file layout License Setup — Preparing your license Quick Start — Protecting your first EXE Project Configuration (JSON) — Project file structure and settings 1. Download & Purchase VxLang is distributed through Patreon. You can purchase and download the product from the following page. Official purchase page: VxLang Patreon Shop Purchase and Download Steps Open the VxLang Shop using the link above. Select the product or license type you need. Review the terms and included items on the product page before purchasing. Follow the instructions for your purchased product to obtain the VxLang distribution files and relevant license materials. Save the downloaded files in your working directory. Note: License duration, update availability, license type, and delivery methods may differ by product. Check the specific product page before purchasing. Do not assume that Patreon memberships and individual Shop purchases are identical products. 2. Installation & File Structure To get started, extract the distributed files into your preferred working directory. VxLang is a Windows application and should be run in a Windows environment. Main Components Component Description VxLang.exe Applies protection such as packing, code obfuscation, and code virtualization to executables. Obscurion.exe GUI tool used to configure projects and protection regions. vxlang.vxm Example license filename (based on the earlier official guide). Extensions VxLang-Core extension code that may be included in the distribution. Plugins Plugin modules used by the GUI and VxLang. SDKs SDK resources used to mark protection regions in source code. Actual file and directory contents may vary depending on the purchased product and distribution version . Not every distribution necessarily includes all the components listed above. Example Working Directory TEXT Copy C:\VxLang\
├── VxLang.exe
├── Obscurion.exe
├── vxlang.vxm          (if a separate license file is supplied)
├── Extensions\         (if included)
├── Plugins\            (if included)
├── SDKs\               (if included)
└── samples\
    └── sample.exe      (a test file provided by the user) This directory layout is illustrative. You do not need to rearrange the original distribution to match it. Recommendation: For your first test, use a simple executable that you created or have already verified works correctly. Keep a backup of the original file and use a distinct filename for the protected output. 3. License Setup A valid license compatible with your distribution is required to run VxLang. The earlier official user guide refers to the license file as vxlang.vxm and instructs users to place it in the same directory as VxLang.exe and Obscurion.exe . TEXT Copy C:\VxLang\
├── VxLang.exe
├── Obscurion.exe
└── vxlang.vxm If your purchased product specifies a different license filename or delivery method, follow the instructions supplied with that product . Verify Startup Open Command Prompt ( cmd ) and run the following commands from the VxLang directory: BAT Copy cd /d "C:\VxLang" VxLang.exe If the program starts successfully, it may display version information and the available command-line syntax. The exact output varies by version. If you encounter a license error, verify the license filename, location, validity period, and compatibility with your distribution. 4. Quick Start — Protecting Your First EXE VxLang can protect compiled EXE files directly from the command line. The following example demonstrates a simple workflow that protects sample.exe and generates sample.vxm.exe . 4.1. Prepare a Test File First, prepare a working Windows executable: TEXT Copy C:\VxLang\samples\sample.exe Confirm that the original sample.exe runs correctly before applying protection. 4.2. Run Protection from the Command Line Open Command Prompt and run: BAT Copy cd /d "C:\VxLang" VxLang.exe "C:\VxLang\samples\sample.exe" --out "C:\VxLang\samples\sample.vxm.exe" Argument Description VxLang.exe The program that performs the protection operation. sample.exe Path to the input binary. --out Specifies the output path for the protected file. This command format is based on the earlier official CLI guide. Refer to your program's help output and documentation for the options and default behavior supported by your version. 4.3. Check the Output After a successful protection operation, verify that the output file exists at the specified location: TEXT Copy C:\VxLang\samples\
├── sample.exe
└── sample.vxm.exe When no output path is provided, the generated filename may append .vxm to the original name. Since this behavior may depend on the version and settings, explicitly specifying the output path with --out is recommended for your first test. 4.4. Run the Protected Executable Run sample.vxm.exe and check that its basic functionality behaves the same as the original. For an initial test, it is best to complete basic protection and runtime verification first , rather than enabling multiple advanced obfuscation or virtualization settings at once. 5. Project Configuration (JSON) VxLang uses JSON files as project files . A project file stores the input binary path, output settings, virtualization and obfuscation regions, packing options, and other protection settings. The example below preserves the structure of the provided temp.json file, with input changed to an empty string ( "" ) as requested. Before running a protection operation, specify the target binary path in input . 5.1. Example Project JSON JSON Tree View Copy { "input" : "" , "output" : "" , "backup" : false , "use-data-section" : false , "base-section-name" : "" , "map-file-path" : "" , "pdb-file-path" : "" , "core-name-list" : [ "vxlang" , "phobos" , "deimos" ], "core-name" : "phobos" , "use-cet-mode" : false , "virtualizer" : { "entry-point" : false , "machine-count" : 3 , "virtualization" : [], "dual-mode" : [] }, "obfuscator" : { "entry-point" : false , "function-entry" : false , "obfuscation" : [], "flattening" : [] }, "protector" : { "compress" : true , "symbol-data" : false , "mutate-import-table" : true , "remove-import-table" : true , "allow-wine-system" : false , "extension" : [], "raw-data" : [], "anti-tamper" : { "enable" : false , "enable-integrity-check" : false , "message" : "" }, "reflection" : { "enable" : false , "ldr-update" : false } }, "address-range" : [] } Note: This example illustrates the project configuration structure . Arrays such as virtualization , obfuscation , extension , and address-range are empty in the supplied source file, so their individual item schemas cannot be determined from this example alone. Follow the configuration specifications for your VxLang version. 5.2. General Project Settings Setting Type Description input String Path to the input binary to protect. Left empty ( "" ) in this example as requested. output String Output path for the protected binary. Confirm the automatic naming rules for an empty value ( "" ) in your version. backup Boolean Option related to backing up the original file. Accepts true or false . use-data-section Boolean Controls whether a data section is used. Exact placement behavior depends on the version. base-section-name String Specifies the base name of sections being generated or processed. map-file-path String Path to a MAP symbol file. pdb-file-path String Path to a PDB debug-symbol file. core-name-list Array of strings Names of available cores for the project. This example contains vxlang , phobos , and deimos . core-name String Name of the selected obfuscation core. This example uses phobos . use-cet-mode Boolean Enables a CET-compatible execution mode. Actual support depends on the environment and version. About core-name : In the current VxLang configuration, core-name selects the core for general code obfuscation and obfuscation APIs. It does not select the entire packer shell or virtualization VM handlers. phobos is recommended for general use. Depending on the version, deimos may have compatibility or performance limitations. 5.3. virtualizer — Code Virtualization Settings Setting Type Description virtualizer.entry-point Boolean Controls whether virtualization is applied to the program entry point. virtualizer.machine-count Number Specifies the number of VM configurations used by the project. The example value is 3 . virtualizer.virtualization Array List of regions configured for standard code virtualization. virtualizer.dual-mode Array List of regions configured for Dual-Mode protection. The item formats of these two arrays (for example, how addresses, functions, or ranges are specified) are not established here because temp.json provides no populated examples. 5.4. obfuscator — Code Obfuscation Settings Setting Type Description obfuscator.entry-point Boolean Controls obfuscation of the program entry point. obfuscator.function-entry Boolean Controls obfuscation of function entry regions. obfuscator.obfuscation Array List of regions targeted for general code obfuscation. obfuscator.flattening Array List of regions targeted for control flow flattening. 5.5. protector — Packer and Executable Protection Settings Setting Type Description protector.compress Boolean Enables or disables compression during protection. protector.symbol-data Boolean Option related to symbol-data processing. Refer to the version-specific specification for details. protector.mutate-import-table Boolean Enables or disables Import Table mutation. protector.remove-import-table Boolean Configures processing related to Import Table removal. protector.allow-wine-system Boolean Controls whether the Wine execution environment is allowed. protector.extension Array Configuration list for protection extensions or modules. protector.raw-data Array Configuration list for additional raw data. mutate-import-table and remove-import-table are separate settings. Verify their availability and combined behavior in your version. Anti-Tamper Settings Setting Type Description protector.anti-tamper.enable Boolean Enables or disables Anti-Tamper protection. protector.anti-tamper.enable-integrity-check Boolean Enables or disables integrity checking. protector.anti-tamper.message String Specifies an Anti-Tamper-related message. Display conditions depend on the implementation. Reflection Settings Setting Type Description protector.reflection.enable Boolean Enables or disables the Reflection feature. protector.reflection.ldr-update Boolean Configures LDR-update behavior associated with Reflection. Refer to the dedicated feature specifications for exact behavior and prerequisites. 5.6. address-range — Address Range Settings Setting Type Description address-range Array Configuration list for address ranges specified in the project. In the supplied JSON, address-range is an empty array ( [] ). Since the file does not define the fields or precedence rules for individual address-range objects, no speculative item format is added here. 5.7. Project File Guidelines Enter the actual target binary path in input before using the project. The example in this guide leaves it empty. In JSON, enclose strings in double quotes ( " ) and write Boolean values as true or false . Escape backslashes ( \ ) when entering Windows paths directly in JSON strings. Example: "C:\\VxLang\\sample.exe" . An empty array ( [] ) means no items are specified in that array. It does not necessarily mean other related settings are automatically disabled. Consider backing up your JSON file before modifying the project configuration so you can compare or restore settings.

title: Protection Features
text:
Protection Features VxLang provides Code Obfuscation , Code Virtualization , Code Flattening , Runtime Code Encryption , and Packer & Protector to protect code and data in Windows executables. This document first explains the SDK markers used to designate protected regions in C/C++ source code, then introduces the purpose and characteristics of each protection method. For detailed JSON settings, see Project Configuration (JSON) . 1. SDK Protection Markers 1.1. Overview The VxLang SDK provides BEGIN/END markers for designating regions of C/C++ code to protect. By placing markers around the intended code, VxLang can identify the corresponding region during protection. The supplied vxlib.h declares the following markers: Protection method Begin marker End marker Description Code Obfuscation VL_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN VL_OBFUSCATION_END General code obfuscation Lite Obfuscation VL_LITE_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN VL_LITE_OBFUSCATION_END Region for lightweight obfuscation Code Flattening VL_CODE_FLATTENING_BEGIN VL_CODE_FLATTENING_END Control-flow obfuscation Code Virtualization VL_VIRTUALIZATION_BEGIN VL_VIRTUALIZATION_END VM-based virtualization Dual-Mode VL_DUAL_MODE_BEGIN VL_DUAL_MODE_END Combined protection mode TMA Virtualization / Super Operators VL_TMA_VIRTUALIZATION_BEGIN VL_TMA_VIRTUALIZATION_END TMA virtualization using Super Operators Runtime Code Encryption VL_ENCRYPT_BEGIN VL_ENCRYPT_END User code section encryption Runtime Encryption + Obfuscation VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_END Combined encryption and obfuscation for VxLang code sections Note: TMA Virtualization and Super Operators refer to the same protection feature in this documentation; they are not presented as separate features. 1.2. SDK Header and Macro Activation When USE_VL_MACRO is defined and vxlib.h is included, protection marker macros expand into SDK function calls such as VxVirtualizationBegin() . CPP Copy #define USE_VL_MACRO #include "vxlib.h" If USE_VL_MACRO is not defined, the protection-region BEGIN/END macros expand to nothing in the provided header. Make sure this setting is enabled in builds that should contain the protection markers. Builds that invoke SDK functions also require the appropriate linkage and implementation. The integration procedure is covered in SDK Integration . 1.3. Code Protection Example The following example marks a portion of a function for virtualization: CPP Copy #define USE_VL_MACRO #include "vxlib.h" int CalculateValue ( int value ) { int result = 0 ; VL_VIRTUALIZATION_BEGIN ; result = ( value * 7 ) + 13 ; VL_VIRTUALIZATION_END ; return result ; } Place BEGIN/END markers so that they enclose the code you actually want to protect . For general obfuscation, use VL_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN / VL_OBFUSCATION_END . For TMA virtualization, use VL_TMA_VIRTUALIZATION_BEGIN / VL_TMA_VIRTUALIZATION_END . 1.4. Runtime Code Encryption Markers Runtime encryption decrypts a protected code region when it is needed for execution and re-encrypts it when use is complete. CPP Copy VL_ENCRYPT_BEGIN ; // User code to protect VL_ENCRYPT_END ; To combine obfuscation and runtime encryption for a VxLang code section, use: CPP Copy VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN ; // Code to protect VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_END ; According to vxlib.h , the combined markers expand in this order: begin obfuscation → begin encryption ; on exit, end encryption → end obfuscation . Runtime Code Encryption depends on integration with VxLang-Core. 1.5. String Link Events vxlib.h also provides link-event macros for strings and resource release. Macro Purpose VL_ALLOC_STR(str) Invokes an ANSI string-related link event VL_ALLOC_WSTR(str) Invokes a wide-string-related link event VL_FREE(value) Requests release of a resource allocated through a link event Unlike the protection-region markers, these are APIs that return values or manage resources . When USE_VL_MACRO is disabled, these macros expand to nothing, so code using the string APIs must account for the selected build configuration. See SDK Integration for detailed string-handling and return-value rules. 1.6. Usage Notes Use BEGIN/END markers in pairs, and be careful with branches or early exits that leave a protected region. Compiler optimization and inlining can cause the generated machine-code region to differ from the source-code region. Prefer important functions or sensitive code regions over performance-critical loops. For VL_ENCRYPT_* markers, verify correct BEGIN/END execution and multithreaded behavior. The marker names and macro expansion behavior described here are based on the supplied vxlib.h . 2. Protection Methods Overview Protection method Primary target Main purpose Packer & Protector Overall executable structure and loading process Packing, protection of file structure and sensitive information, integrity checking Code Obfuscation Selected functions or instruction regions Make code representation and analysis structure more complex Code Virtualization Selected critical code regions Transform native code into a virtual-instruction execution model Code Flattening Function control flow Increase the difficulty of analyzing branches and execution flow Runtime Code Encryption Designated code regions Decrypt only when needed and re-encrypt after use Note: Availability and detailed behavior may vary depending on the VxLang version, target environment, and configuration. 3. Packer & Protector 3.1. Overview Packer & Protector protects a target binary's structure and loading process. It works together with VxLang-Core to run protected executables and can include features such as compression and Import Table protection. This is the basic configuration typically used when applying protection to an entire program. 3.2. Executable Packing Executable Packing transforms a target binary into VxLang's protected format. Protected executables run through VxLang-Core initialization and execution flow. Key characteristics Adds a protected loading structure to the executable. Makes direct analysis of the original executable structure and entry process more difficult. Can be combined with other code-protection methods. 3.3. Compression Compression compresses executable data. It can be enabled or disabled in the project configuration. JSON Tree View Copy { "protector" : { "compress" : true } } true : Enable compression. false : Disable compression. Compression is part of the protected-file format; compression alone does not prevent analysis of the code itself. The resulting file size can vary with the compression ratio and the additional protection code. 3.4. Import Table Protection The Import Table in a Windows PE file contains information about external libraries and APIs used by the application. VxLang provides options to transform the Import Table structure or protect associated information. Project option Description mutate-import-table Enables Import Table mutation. remove-import-table Enables the Import Table removal-related feature. These features are intended to make it harder to identify external API dependencies through static analysis. Verify the actual effect of enabling both options for your target binary and VxLang version. 3.5. Entry Point Protection The Entry Point is where program execution begins. Protecting this region can make analysis of the initial execution path more difficult. VxLang can configure virtualization or obfuscation of the Entry Point through project settings. virtualizer.entry-point : Entry Point virtualization obfuscator.entry-point : Entry Point obfuscation Specific behavior and support conditions may depend on the target file. Verify startup and shutdown behavior after applying protection. 3.6. Anti-Tamper Protection Anti-Tamper is designed to detect or respond to unauthorized modifications to protected applications. The supplied project format includes: Project option Description protector.anti-tamper.enable Enables Anti-Tamper. protector.anti-tamper.enable-integrity-check Enables integrity checking. protector.anti-tamper.message Sets the message displayed on detection. This feature does not guarantee detection of every modification or analysis attempt . It can be used alongside other safeguards, including code signing, distribution-file verification, and server-side validation. 3.7. Reflection Reflection is a protection option that adjusts aspects of executable loading. protector.reflection.enable : Enables Reflection. protector.reflection.ldr-update : Controls updating Windows loader-management (LDR) information. Compatibility testing may be necessary with security software that interacts with the loader and in certain execution environments. 4. Code Obfuscation 4.1. Overview Code Obfuscation changes the representation and structure of instructions while preserving the behavior of the program's operations. Its purpose is to maintain the same results while complicating static analysis, pattern matching, and automated code interpretation. VxLang can apply obfuscation to selected functions or code regions. 4.2. Instruction Transformation Instruction transformation replaces existing instructions with semantically equivalent sequences. For example, it may split simple arithmetic or logic operations into multiple operations, introduce intermediate calculations, or change instruction arrangements. Results depend on the selected protection core and options. 4.3. MBA Obfuscation MBA (Mixed Boolean-Arithmetic) combines arithmetic and Boolean operations to express an original calculation in a more complex form. Expected benefits Makes the meaning of code harder to recognize directly. Complicates simple instruction-pattern matching. Can increase the effort needed to analyze and simplify expressions. Applying more MBA transformations can increase code size and execution time. 4.4. Function-Level Obfuscation Function-level obfuscation protects the implementation of selected functions, such as license checks, critical calculations, and security validation. The obfuscator.obfuscation array stores the selection information for code regions to obfuscate. The format of individual array entries is described in Project Configuration . The obfuscator.function-entry option configures obfuscation associated with function entry points. 4.5. Protection Core Selection VxLang uses the core-name setting to select a protection core for general obfuscation. Core Description Recommendation phobos Default protection core Recommended for general use deimos Core designed to provide polymorphic hash-based MBA obfuscation Check compatibility during ongoing core improvements vxlang Core name included in the project configuration Verify support in the distributed version The currently recommended core is phobos . If core-name is omitted, phobos is used by default. In the current core architecture, core-name applies to general obfuscation and the obfuscation API; it does not select the core used by the Packer Shell or VM Handlers. deimos may increase code-block splitting and affect performance, and it may be incompatible during core refactoring. 5. Code Virtualization 5.1. Overview Code Virtualization converts selected native code into VxLang's virtual-instruction format. A VxLang virtual execution engine is used to execute protected code. By adding a translation layer between the original machine instructions and the virtual instructions handled at runtime, virtualization aims to make direct reconstruction of the original algorithm and control flow more difficult. 5.2. Virtual Machine-Based Protection A typical protection flow is: TEXT Copy Original Native Code
        |
        v
VxLang Virtualization
        |
        v
Virtual Instructions + VM Execution Engine
        |
        v
Protected Code Execution The selected code region is handled by VxLang's virtual execution model. This transformation can make it harder to understand the code's behavior using native-code analysis alone. 5.3. Multiple Virtual Machines VxLang supports configurations using multiple virtual machines. The supplied project file contains: virtualizer.machine-count : Setting related to the number of virtual machines. Using more than one VM does not automatically guarantee stronger protection; code size and execution overhead should also be considered. 5.4. Dual-Mode Protection Dual-Mode combines Code Obfuscation and Code Virtualization for selected code. TEXT Copy Selected Code
     |
     v
Obfuscation + Virtualization
     |
     v
Protected Execution It can add complexity compared with virtualization alone, but may also affect performance and binary size. Use virtualizer.dual-mode to specify protected regions. 5.5. TMA Virtualization (Super Operators) TMA Virtualization and Super Operators are the same feature. VxLang provides its Super Operator-based execution model under the name TMA Virtualization. They are not separate virtualization options. Use the following SDK markers in C/C++: VL_TMA_VIRTUALIZATION_BEGIN VL_TMA_VIRTUALIZATION_END TMA has a distinct SDK interface from standard virtualization. Check support requirements and runtime performance with your target application and distributed version. 5.6. Performance Considerations Virtualization can add processing overhead compared with native instruction execution. Performance degradation may be particularly noticeable when applied broadly to frequently called code or tight loops. Recommendation: Apply virtualization selectively to critical algorithms, validation logic, and high-priority code regions, then compare performance before and after protection. 6. Code Flattening 6.1. Overview Code Flattening (Control Flow Flattening) is an obfuscation method that transforms a program's branch and execution-flow structure. It complicates analysis of the original function's control flow and execution order. 6.2. Control Flow Transformation Use obfuscator.flattening in the project to specify regions for this protection. Typical functions have relatively recognizable branch graphs formed by conditions and loops. Code Flattening can restructure these flows using state-based dispatch or similar constructs, making the original control flow more difficult to read directly. TEXT Copy Before

 Entry
   |
 Condition
  /     \
 A       B
  \     /
    Exit

After (conceptual)

   Entry
     |
  Dispatcher <----+
   /    \         |
 State A State B --+
     |
    Exit This is a conceptual illustration; the generated control flow will not necessarily have exactly this structure. 6.3. Usage Considerations Prioritize functions where protection is most valuable instead of applying flattening indiscriminately. Output code size and execution time may vary with function size and complexity. Test protected functions that contain branches, loops, exception handling, and compiler optimizations. 7. Runtime Code Encryption 7.1. Overview Runtime Code Encryption keeps designated code regions encrypted, decrypts them when execution is required, and re-encrypts them after use . It is designed to account for analysis of process memory at runtime as well as examination of the executable on disk. 7.2. Encryption Lifecycle TEXT Copy Encrypted Code (at rest)
        |
        | BEGIN
        v
Decrypted Code (in use)
        |
        | Protected code executes
        v
END
        |
        v
Re-encrypted Code BEGIN: Decrypts the protected code region so it can execute. Protected Execution: The decrypted code performs its required operations. END: Re-encrypts the designated protected region. There may be an interval during execution when protected code exists in plaintext. Therefore, Runtime Code Encryption does not mean that original code can never appear in memory . 7.3. VxLang-Core Dependency Runtime Code Encryption is designed to operate together with VxLang-Core . Removing the Packer Shell from a protected executable does not automatically restore the encrypted original code or make it executable. The required VxLang-Core components must be loaded to decrypt and execute encrypted code. This is an important distinction between unpacking an executable and recovering its original code. 7.4. Protected Code Types The SDK can designate regions for Runtime Code Encryption. Protected region SDK macros User code section protection VL_ENCRYPT_BEGIN / VL_ENCRYPT_END VxLang code section protection VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN / VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_END The VxLang code section protection API can also be used in configurations with Axion memory protection. Actual declarations, linking requirements, and examples are covered in SDK Integration . 7.5. Thread-Safe Execution Runtime Code Encryption is designed around reference counting to account for cases where multiple threads use the same encrypted code region. This is intended to prevent premature re-encryption while a thread is still executing the code. Test nested protected regions and thread-termination scenarios in the target application. 7.6. Protection Benefits Hinders code collection through memory dumps Code stays encrypted when not in use, which may make it harder to capture all original code in a protected region from a memory dump taken at an arbitrary moment. Increases dynamic analysis effort An analyst may need to track the precise decryption and execution windows, requiring more work than conventional bulk dumping and code collection. Separates unpacking from original-code recovery The VxLang-Core-dependent encryption design can restrict decryption and execution even after the Packer Shell has been removed. Increases the difficulty of AI-assisted analysis By limiting the time and scope in which plaintext code is available, the feature may make automated code collection and subsequent analysis more difficult. It does not, however, completely conceal code exposed during execution or the results of execution. 8. Choosing a Protection Method Consider the following options based on what you need to protect. Goal Feature to consider first Baseline protection for the entire executable Packer & Protector Increase analysis difficulty for ordinary functions Code Obfuscation Protect critical algorithms or validation logic Code Virtualization Combine virtualization and obfuscation Dual-Mode Protect branching and control-flow structure Code Flattening Minimize continuous exposure of code during execution Runtime Code Encryption Combine methods for critical functions Evaluate compatible combinations of Virtualization / Obfuscation / Runtime Code Encryption Recommended approach: Start with baseline executable protection, selectively add obfuscation or virtualization to critical functions, and apply Runtime Code Encryption where needed. Choose combinations based on actual feature support and performance testing. 9. Important Considerations Performance: Some protection methods increase execution time, memory usage, or output file size. Compatibility: Certain options may be limited by the OS, CPU, compiler, exception-handling model, or target binary structure. Compiler optimization: With SDK BEGIN/END regions, compiler code movement or merging may cause the actual protected region to differ from the intended one. Feature combinations: Options apply at different execution layers, so not all combinations are supported in the same way. Validation: After protection, test startup, shutdown, primary functionality, multithreading, exception handling, and performance in the actual deployment environment. 10. Related Documentation Getting Started — Installation and creation of your first project Project Configuration (JSON) — Protection options and project fields Using Obscurion (GUI) — Selecting protected regions through the GUI SDK Integration — Designating protected code regions in C/C++ Advanced Configuration — Advanced settings for performance and compatibility This is a user-facing overview of VxLang protection features. Refer to the configuration and API reference for your distributed version to confirm the exact feature support and option usage.

title: VxLang SDK Tutorial — Precautions
text: VxLang SDK Tutorial — Precautions This document explains compiler behavior and control-flow considerations when applying VxLang SDK protection markers. Precautions — Essential Considerations Before Using the SDK The VxLang SDK uses BEGIN and END markers to designate regions of code for protection. The actual machine code and control flow generated by a compiler may differ from the C/C++ source structure. Before defining a protected region, review the following four considerations. 1. Compiler Optimization When compiler optimizations are enabled, the compiler may eliminate unnecessary code, merge duplicate code, or rearrange instructions. As a result, the instructions between SDK markers may not match the intended region and could cause runtime issues. We recommend disabling optimization only for functions that use SDK protection markers and verifying the compiled output. MSVC supports #pragma optimize("", off) , while Clang supports #pragma clang optimize off . 2. Jump Tables and Indirect Branches A switch-case statement may be compiled into jump-table-based control flow that uses indirect jumps, such as jmp reg or jumps through memory. If an indirect branch crosses an unexpected boundary of a protected region, problems may occur. We recommend applying separate SDK markers to the executable code in each case rather than wrapping the entire function . Inspect the actual branch structure generated by the compiler. 3. Windows SEH Exception Handling Structured Exception Handling (SEH) can redirect control flow along exception paths rather than normal sequential execution. For code that uses SEH, the official guidance describes enclosing both the __try and __except blocks within the SDK marker pair . Verify correct behavior for your compiler, architecture, and selected protection mode. 4. Compiler-Specific Language Exception Handling Language-level exception handling, including C++, depends on compiler-specific metadata and stack-unwinding rules. We recommend placing the actual throw statement outside SDK markers , while protecting the ordinary execution code within try and catch separately where needed. Support may depend on the compiler and the applicable VxLang plugin. The following sections provide examples and additional details for each consideration. 1. Compiler Optimization Considerations When optimization is enabled, a compiler may remove unnecessary instructions, merge duplicate code, or change the layout of instructions inside a function. This may affect the intended protection region defined by SDK BEGIN / END markers. We recommend disabling optimization for the protected function and checking the final compiler output. MSVC CPP Copy #pragma optimize("", off) void Test () { VL_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN ; // Protected code VL_OBFUSCATION_END ; } #pragma optimize("", on) #pragma optimize("", off) disables optimization for subsequent function definitions. #pragma optimize("", on) re-enables the specified optimization settings for subsequent functions. In this example, the directives are positioned so that only Test() is affected. If the project uses different optimization settings, take care to restore the intended configuration. Clang / Clang-CL CPP Copy #pragma clang optimize off void Test () { VL_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN ; // Protected code VL_OBFUSCATION_END ; } #pragma clang optimize on Clang allows optimization to be controlled around function definitions with #pragma clang optimize off/on . You can also apply the optnone attribute to an individual function: CPP Copy __attribute__ (( optnone )) void Test () { VL_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN ; // Protected code VL_OBFUSCATION_END ; } Note: Disabling optimization does not automatically control every compiler-generated branch, jump table, or function boundary. Inspect the generated assembly and test the executable after applying markers. 2. Jump Table-Based Branch Transition The compiler may implement branching constructs such as switch-case using indirect jumps or jump tables. For example, it may generate patterns such as jmp reg or jmp [reg+reg+offset] , where the destination is selected through a register or memory. If a branch inside a protected region transfers control outside that region or to an unexpected location, the protection transformation may interfere with execution. Therefore, rather than wrapping an entire function, we recommend placing BEGIN / END markers around the actual executable code of each case . CPP Copy void Test ( int value ) { switch ( value ) { case 1 : VL_VIRTUALIZATION_BEGIN ; DoCaseOne (); VL_VIRTUALIZATION_END ; break ; case 2 : VL_VIRTUALIZATION_BEGIN ; DoCaseTwo (); VL_VIRTUALIZATION_END ; break ; default : VL_VIRTUALIZATION_BEGIN ; DoDefault (); VL_VIRTUALIZATION_END ; break ; } } DoCaseOne , DoCaseTwo , and DoDefault are illustrative user-defined functions. Ensure that each control-flow path has matching BEGIN / END markers, and avoid jumping directly from a protected region into a different case. Verify compatibility and performance in the final executable. 3. Exception Handling — SEH Windows Structured Exception Handling (SEH) transfers control along exception paths that differ from normal sequential execution. The official guidance illustrates a protected SEH region by enclosing the entire exception-handling construct within SDK markers. CPP Copy #pragma optimize("", off) void Test () { VL_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN ; __try { // Protected operation } __except ( EXCEPTION_EXECUTE_HANDLER ) { // Handle the exception } VL_OBFUSCATION_END ; } #pragma optimize("", on) This example assumes Windows SEH and a compiler environment that supports it. Verify the supported behavior for your target architecture and VxLang version. 4. Compiler-Specific Exception Handling — C++ / Rust / Other Languages Language-level exception handling, including C++, depends on compiler-generated exception metadata and unwinding code. Unlike ordinary branching, this may affect the boundaries of protected regions. The official guidance recommends placing the statement that actually throws an exception outside the SDK markers . The following example protects ordinary code within try and catch separately while keeping the throw outside the protected region. CPP Copy #include <stdexcept> void Test () { try { VL_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN ; // Protected operation VL_OBFUSCATION_END ; throw std :: runtime_error ( "Example exception" ); } catch (...) { VL_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN ; // Protected exception-handling code VL_OBFUSCATION_END ; } } Note: This example demonstrates the intended marker boundaries; it does not guarantee compatibility with every compiler or exception type. Exception-handling support may vary depending on the compiler implementation and the corresponding VxLang plugin. 5. SDK Integration Checklist Confirm that every normal execution path contains properly matched BEGIN / END markers. Disable optimization only for functions that require it. Verify that jump tables and indirect jumps do not cross unexpected protection boundaries. Review the boundaries of exception-throwing code and exception-handling blocks. Test actual behavior in both Debug and Release builds. Verify functionality and performance in the protected executable. This tutorial covers precautions to review before using the SDK. For specific API declarations, refer to vxlib.h and the separate Protection Features documentation.

title: VxLang SDK Tutorial — Linking with VxLang-Core
text: VxLang SDK Tutorial — Linking with VxLang-Core Overview Runtime Code Encryption is a VxLang protection feature that decrypts the code of a designated function only when it is needed for execution and re-encrypts it when the protected region is no longer in use. This tutorial explains how to link function-level code protection with VxLang-Core (the packer core) using the SDK markers VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN and VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_END . This approach is designed to make it harder to recover the original protected code in a single operation, even if the packer shell is removed through static unpacking or the running process is dumped from memory. Because the decrypted state depends on execution timing and VxLang-Core operation, AI-assisted dynamic analysis also requires additional steps to collect and reconstruct the code. Important: The goal is not to make analysis impossible. It is to reduce the duration and scope of plaintext code exposure and increase the difficulty of collecting code through static and dynamic analysis. 1. How Runtime Code Encryption Works With conventional executable packing, it may be possible to inspect or dump executable code from memory after unpacking. Runtime Code Encryption reduces this exposure by decrypting code when it is needed and re-encrypting it afterward . Distribution: The designated protected code is stored in encrypted form. Execution preparation: When a protected function is needed, its code is decrypted in coordination with VxLang-Core. Protected code execution: The decrypted code executes within the required region. Completion: Once the protected region is no longer in use, the code is encrypted again. VxLang-Core dependency: VxLang-Core must be loaded and operating for protected code to be decrypted and executed correctly. Removing only the packer shell does not automatically recover the original code or make it independently executable. 2. SDK Example First, include the VxLang SDK header in your project and enable SDK markers. CPP Copy #define USE_VL_MACRO #include "vxlib.h" void LinkTest () { VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN ; // Code to protect in conjunction with VxLang-Core volatile int value = 10 ; value = value * 2 + 5 ; ( void ) value ; VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_END ; } When USE_VL_MACRO is enabled, the two markers are defined in the provided SDK header as follows: CPP Copy #define VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN VxObfuscationBegin(); VxLinkExtsBegin() #define VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_END   VxLinkExtsEnd(); VxObfuscationEnd() These markers designate both an Obfuscation protection region and a Runtime Code Encryption protection region . The example demonstrates how to place the SDK markers; the actual protection transformation is performed during the VxLang build process. If USE_VL_MACRO is not defined, these markers expand to empty macros. Make sure the SDK markers are enabled in your protection build. 3. Protection Benefits Analysis scenario Expected benefit Static Unpacking Removing the packer shell alone does not readily expose the original code in the Runtime Code Encryption region. Memory Dumping Because protected code is not continuously present in plaintext form, collecting all of it through a single memory snapshot becomes more difficult. AI-Assisted Dynamic Analysis Automated code collection and analysis become more complex because the decrypted execution state and its interaction with VxLang-Core must be tracked. Static Analysis Encrypting protected regions in the distributed binary makes direct analysis of their original machine instructions more difficult. These benefits vary depending on the analysis environment and the code being protected. Decrypted code may still be observed dynamically while it is executing. This feature does not guarantee that all dumping, tracing, or reconstruction attempts will be blocked. 4. Important Considerations VxLang-Core is required. Do not assume that code protected with Runtime Code Encryption can be decrypted and executed independently without VxLang-Core. Place BEGIN/END markers correctly. Both markers should clearly enclose the intended code region within the same function. Be careful with exceptions and abnormal control flow. Code that exits the protected region unexpectedly through return , an exception, or a long jump requires additional testing. Test multithreaded behavior. The feature is designed with reference-count-based thread safety in mind, but concurrent calls and reentrancy must still be tested in the actual application. Watch for compiler optimization and function inlining. Verify that the intended SDK protection boundaries remain intact in the compiled binary. Limit optimization for the affected function when necessary. Measure compatibility and performance. Decryption and re-encryption introduce runtime costs as well as protection benefits. Benchmark functions that are called very frequently before enabling this feature. 5. Summary VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_BEGIN / VL_ENCRYPT_OBFUSCATION_END are SDK markers that designate both code obfuscation and Runtime Code Encryption . By working with VxLang-Core to decrypt the original code only when needed, they add a layer of defense against attempts to recover code through static unpacking alone , bulk memory dumping , and AI-assisted automated dynamic analysis . The central principle is: Unpacking the executable does not mean recovering the original code. VxLang SDK Tutorial · Runtime Code Encryption

title: Q&A
text: Q&A If you have any questions about VxLang, please contact the developer directly via email. Contact Email: 0x999h@gmail.com Inquiries You are welcome to contact us regarding: General questions about VxLang License purchases and subscription policies Installation and SDK integration Protection features and configuration Technical issues and bug reports Team Named License purchase inquiries Feature requests and improvement suggestions Technical Support When reporting a technical issue, please provide the following information where applicable: VxLang version Operating system and target architecture Compiler and compiler version Protection settings Error messages and steps to reproduce the issue Sample code that reproduces the issue (required for crashes or unexpected behavior) When reporting a crash or unexpected behavior, you must attach a minimal sample code that reproduces the same issue to facilitate reproduction and root cause analysis. Where possible, isolate the sample code from your actual project and ensure that the issue can be reproduced using the same protection settings. Please do not include your license file, confidential source code, or other sensitive information in your initial inquiry. VxLang is developed and maintained by an independent developer. Response times may vary depending on the nature of the inquiry and the development schedule. Thank you for your interest in and support of VxLang. Contact the Developer
